questions.explanation: In hospital studies, the mean age of onset is 21 years while it is 17 years in community studies

questions.question_text: Which of the following physiological changes often produce an arti�cially elevated calcium level in blood?
questions.explanation:
Only one half of the exchangeable calcium in blood is in the active ionized form with the remainder bound to albumin, globulin, and other
inorganic molecules. Protein binding of calcium is in�uenced by pH with metabolic acidosis leading to increased ionized calcium from
reduced protein binding, and alkalosis leading to reduced ionized calcium from increased protein binding. Because calcium binds to albumin
and only the unbound (free or ionized) calcium is biologically active, the serum level must be adjusted for abnormal albumin levels. For every
1-g/dL drop in serum albumin below 4 g/dL, measured serum calcium decreases by 0.8 mg/dL. Therefore, to correct for an albumin level of
less than 4 g/dL, one should add 0.8 to the measured value of calcium for each 1-g/dL decrease in albumin. Without this correction, an
abnormally high serum calcium level may appear to be normal. (From

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressant must be avoided in a patient with breast cancer taking tamoxifen?
questions.explanation:
Paroxetine, �uoxetine, duloxetine and bupropion are strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, which should be avoided in tamoxifen users. Amitriptyline
and its metabolite, nortriptyline, are metabolized by and can inhibit CYP2D6. Fluvoxamine and nefazodone both inhibit CYP3A, which could
potentially a�ect the metabolism of tamoxifen. Venlafaxine has little or no e�ect on the metabolism of tamoxifen and may be considered
the safest choice of antidepressants. Mirtazapine has not been extensively studied, but existing research suggests minimal e�ect on
CYP2D6. The remaining commonly prescribed antidepressants have mild to moderate degrees of CYP2D6 inhibition. (Excerpt retrieved from
Desmaraias & Looper 2010  )

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants is preferable to be used in a patient who has a history of gastrointestinal bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Patients on predominant serotonergic reuptake inhibiting (SRI) antidepressants (HIGH RISK: paroxetine, �uoxetine, sertraline, and
clomipramine, MODERATE RISK: amitriptyline, venlafaxine) have a greater risk of developing upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding compared
with those taking low-SRI antidepressants (LOW RISK: mirtazapine, bupropion, nortriptyline, desipramine). This risk was even higher among
patients with a history of GI bleeding. Ref: Meijer WE., et al. Association of risk of abnormal bleeding with degree of serotonin reuptake
inhibition by antidepressants. Arch Intern Med 2004;164:2367 –2370

questions.question_text: The most common type of personality disorder in the community is
questions.explanation:
Patients with Cluster C personality disorders are the commonest personality disorders to be encountered among primary care attenders
(Moran et al. 2000). When ICD diagnoses are considered individually, anankastic personality is the most common type of primary care,
followed by impulsive (emotionally unstable) type.

questions.question_text:
Mark has chronic pain and depression, which is not responding to SSRI antidepressants. Which one of the following is the best
antidepressant of choice in this situation?
questions.explanation:
As this patient has not responded to SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants like Amitriptyline would be a good choice. Amitriptyline is also
prescribed frequently for the treatment of neuropathic pain.

questions.question_text:
Tom is a middle-aged gentleman with a history of depression and has had erectile dysfunction with SSRIs. You are willing to add another
drug to reduce sexual side e�ects of his current medication. What is the most appropriate drug?
questions.explanation:
Preliminary data support the reduction/reversal of sexual side e�ects in patients taking SSRIs or duloxetine upon addition of Mirtazapine.
Erectile and orgasmic dysfunctions are less common with Mirtazapine. (Ref: Ozmenler NK et al. Mirtazapine augmentation in depressed
patients with sexual dysfunction due to SSRIs, Hum psychopharmacology 2008; 23: 321-326)

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric presentation among the following conditions that is seen in those with cancer is
questions.explanation:
Prevalence of major depression in those with advanced cancer is about 5 –15%. About 10 –15% of cancer patients present with less severe
symptoms. The prevalence of depression in advanced disease is closer to 33% (Hotopf et al. 2001). Somatic symptoms are not useful when
diagnosing depression in the physically ill. Pervasive global anhedonia is a more valid criterion for the diagnosis of depression.

questions.question_text: The most commonly admitted hallucinatory experience among respondents of general population surveys in UK is

options.text: Hearing or seeing things that no one else could experience
Vision of Angel or God while going to sleep
External voices speaking in meaningful sentences

correct_answer.text: Hearing or seeing things that no one else could experience

questions.explanation: Proportion of general population with highly speci�c hallucinatory experience such as voices is very low.

questions.question_text: The one-week prevalence of generalized anxiety disorder according to National Psychiatric Morbidity Survey is
questions.explanation: The one week prevalence of generalized anxiety disorder according to National psychiatric morbidity survey is 3.1%

questions.question_text: Which of the following is indicative of epileptic rather than non-epileptic �ts?
questions.explanation:
Psychogenic non-epileptic attacks are often precipitated by stressful circumstances and in response to suggestion. They may occur in
wakefulness and in the presence of witnesses and lack stereotypic patterns (asynchronous, asymmetrical, waxing and waning, often with
pelvic thrusts, �ailing and tremors). These may be interrupted or resistant to restraint. Attempts to open the eyes passively often result in
tightening of the eyelids. Consciousness may be retained throughout and there is often no actual postictal confusion. The patient may
become emotional and cry after the end of the nonepileptic seizure. After a generalised tonic clonic seizure the corneal re�ex will usually be
impaired and plantar responses extensor. These are commonly absent in nonepileptic seizures.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antipsychotic drug is most likely to cause orthostatic hypotension?
questions.explanation: Risperidone can cause signi�cant �rst-dose orthostatic hypotension which can recur every time during a dose increase.

questions.question_text: Which of the following rating scales includes a physical examination?
questions.explanation: SAS is a scale for assessing extra pyramidal symptoms - hence it requires a physical examination to be completed.

questions.question_text: A 36-year-old man with a history of alcohol dependent syndrome is clinically depressed. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
If a patient has problem-drinking pattern with alcohol and feels suicidal, SSRIs like sertraline are better tolerated and are generally thought
to be safer than, for example, tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), especially due to accidental overdose risk. In addition, the frequency of
adverse e�ects is relatively low, and the severity of most adverse e�ects is mild or moderate.

questions.question_text: Tom is a 7-year-old boy with autistic spectrum disorder. He su�ers from insomnia. The drug of choice is;
questions.explanation:
All forms of insomnia are more common in children with learning di�culties, autism, ADHD and sensory impairments (esp. visual). Although
behavioural interventions should be the primary intervention and have a robust evidence base, exogenous melatonin is now the '�rst-line'
medication prescribed for childhood insomnia. (Ref: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines- 10th edition-pg 279)

questions.question_text: Lucy is a 6-year-old girl who is �ne at home and mute in school. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Elective mutism is a condition in which children demonstrate normal language skills in some situations but fail to speak in others. Typically,
the child speaks with familiar people in familiar surroundings. Eg at home, but fails to speak at school or with strangers.

questions.question_text:
John is a 12-year-old boy with autism and with severe behavioural disturbances. He has been reported as aggressive and violent to
caregivers. The treatment of choice is
questions.explanation:
There is now reasonable evidence for the use of risperidone in the management of aggression, tantrums and self-injury in autistic spectrum
disorder. (Ref: Oxford Handbook of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry- 139)

questions.question_text: A child with Tourette's disorder has had signi�cant weight gain on previous treatment. Which of the following should be o�ered?
questions.explanation:
Weight gain may be more pronounced in children and adolescents than in adults, and this may limit the use of atypicals in young people.
Though there is no established evidence, available case series suggest Aripiprazole is e�ective and well tolerated in children with tics &
Tourette's syndrome. (Ref: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines- 10th edition-pg 277)

questions.question_text:
A 17-year-old girl with a history of anorexia nervosa has a BMI of 14, blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg and has reported two episodes of
fainting. Where will you treat her?
questions.explanation:
BMI less than 14, BP less than 80/60 mm Hg, pulse rate less than 40 beats per minute in patients with anorexia suggests 'high-risk' and such
patients should receive immediate medical treatment. Where there is a choice between medical or psychiatric admission, medical admission
is preferred where risk of feeding syndrome is high and BMI low, allowing more frequent physical monitoring and more immediate
advanced resuscitation facilities than might be available on an eating disorders ward in a psychiatric setting.

questions.question_text: The annual risk of a healthcare professional being stalked by a patient or a patient's relative is
questions.explanation:
The risk of being stalked by a patient or a patient's relative is between 5% and 10% in a year, and around 20% over the course of a career
(Purcell et al, 2005; Mullen et al, 2009). Several surveys of health professionals (summarised by the RCPsych: Retrieved from
 suggest that around 5-11% have been stalked, using a
strict operational de�nition, in a year. There is some variation depending on profession and also within psychiatric subspecialties: for
example, forensic psychiatrists and general adult psychiatrists appear to be at higher risk, whereas the risk seems to be lower for old age
psychiatrists and neuropsychiatrists. (Ref: Royal College of Psychiatrists-2010; Document on Support Service for Psychiatrists).

questions.question_text: What is the relative risk of psychosis in prisons compared to general population?
questions.explanation:
Prisoners were several times (nearly 20 times) more likely to have psychosis and major depression, and about ten times more likely to have
antisocial personality disorder, than the general population (Retrieved from

questions.explanation: Evidence of conduct disorder before the age of 15 is required by the DSM-5.

questions.question_text: How many homicide o�enders have active psychiatric symptoms at the time of committing homicide?
questions.explanation:
Shaw (2006) determined 34% of homicides are related to the mental disorder and 5% of homicides are linked to schizophrenia; 10% of
homicide o�enders have active symptoms at the time of the o�ence.

questions.question_text: In the UK the number of infanticides reported per year is around
questions.explanation:
Under the 1938 Infanticide Act, a woman who kills her child when it is less than a year old and "while the balance of her mind was disturbed
by reason of the fact that she had not fully recovered from the e�ect of giving birth", should not be found guilty of murder. But despite this
Act, many mothers have been found guilty over the recent years. Around 20 cases per year are reported in the UK.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true for female o�enders?

options.text: More likely than males to o�end against family members
Less likely to have a psychiatric disposal
Higher rate of reo�ending than men
Less likely to self harm than men
Violent o�ences are more common than crimes of passion

correct_answer.text: More likely than males to o�end against family members

questions.explanation:
The index o�ence in women is more likely to be 'romantic' or domestic disputes. 68% of women are in prison for non-violent o�ences
(compared with 47% for men). Victims of womens' violent acts are more likely to be family members.

questions.question_text: In females, which of the following age group is associated with the highest risk of committing a homicide?
questions.explanation:
11% of homicide o�enders are women. More than 40% of them fall within the age group 30 to 39 years. The most common victims of female
homicide perpetrators are partners (32%) or son/daughters (30%). Strangers constitute less than 5% of victims killed by female homicide
o�enders.

questions.question_text: With respect to Pritchard criteria for �tness to plead, which of the following need not be demonstrated?

options.text: Ability to understand the outcome of trials of a similar nature that took place in the past.
Ability to follow proceedings of court
Ability to understand the di�erence between pleading guilty vs. not guilty.
Ability to instruct solicitors representing self.

correct_answer.text: Ability to understand the outcome of trials of a similar nature that took place in the past.

questions.explanation:
Pritchard criteria include 1. Ability to understand charges. 2. Ability to follow proceedings 3. Ability to instruct counsel. 4. Ability to
understand the di�erence between pleading guilty vs. not guilty. 5. Ability to challenge juror.

questions.question_text:
You are seeing a 10-year-old boy with a moderate degree of Learning Disability, microcephaly and self-injurious behavior. The most
probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Cornelia De Lange syndrome is one among the causes of learning disability due to lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPPA)
linked to chromosome 9q33. Clinical features include Continuous eyebrows, hypertrichosis, thin down turning upper lip, Prominent
philtrum, small upturned nose, down turned mouth, anteverted nostrils, high arched palate and low set ears, Microcephaly, short stature,
small hands and feet, malformed upper limbs, failure to thrive. Behavioural features include self-injury, limited speech in severe cases,
language delays, avoidance of being held and stereotypic movements.

questions.question_text: According to o�cial crime records, which of the following o�ences is most commonly committed by people with autistic spectrum disorder?
questions.explanation:
People with autistic spectrum disorders are more likely to commit �re-setting and other property-damaging o�ences. The o�ences are
usually a result of poor social skills, co-morbid mental health problems, abuse of drugs and alcohol, or because of their narrow stereotyped
interests.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common feature of fragile-x syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Fragile X speech is often described as "cluttered". Poor topic maintenance with frequent tangential comments may occur. Syntax is usually
appropriate for mental age; a high receptive vocabulary score is usually seen, and auditory sensory and processing skills are weak.

questions.question_text: The incidence of fetal alcohol syndrome is;
questions.explanation:
The worldwide incidence of the fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is 1.9 per 1000 live births. Incidence rates vary considerably, however,
depending on the study site. Mental retardation is a cardinal feature of FAS and is now recognized as the leading known cause of mental
retardation in the Western world. (Ref: Incidence of fetal alcohol syndrome and economic impact of FAS-related anomalies, Abel EL, Sokol RJ)

questions.question_text: A subcultural rather than neuropathological explanation for Learning disability is supported by which of the following?

options.text: Existence of profound degree of learning disability
Even distribution of LD across di�erent socioeconomic groups of the population

questions.explanation:
The following features are suggestive of a Subcultural LD rather than neuropathological explantation - Mild or borderline type, Mild or
borderline type, Family members may also have borderline IQ, Dysmorphic characters less likely, Syndromic features not seen, Behavioural
phenotypes rare

questions.question_text: A 62-year-old man has early signs of dementia. Which of the following suggests a cortical rather than a subcortical origin?
questions.explanation:
Normal alertness is seen in people with cortical dementia like Alzheimer's disease. 'Slowed up' alertness is seen in people with subcortical
dementia like Huntington's disease. Other features of subcortical dementia include impaired attention, impaired executive function,
apathetic & inert personality. Normal praxis is a feature of sub cortical dementia whereas apraxia is seen in cortical dementia. (Ref: Seminars
in Liaison Psychiatry; 2nd edition: pg 170)

questions.question_text: What is the most common medication used for treating patients with Lewy body dementia and psychosis?
questions.explanation:
The �rst line management of cognitive impairment, psychosis and agitation of Lewy body dementia (DLB) and Parkinson's disease dementia
(PDD) is a cholinesterase inhibitor (ChEI). In a large RCT, Rivastigmine alleviated visual hallucinations, delusions, anxiety and apathy in DLB
(McKeith et al 2006). Levodopa induced hallucinations are also less common when ChEIs are co-prescribed. There is a risk of neuroleptic
sensitivity even with atypical antipsychotics of which there are no placebo-controlled trials in DLB. (Ref: Oxford Textbook of Old Age
Psychiatry- pg457)

questions.question_text: The most common behavioural symptom in Alzheimer's disease is;
questions.explanation:
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) refer to the often distressing non-cognitive symptoms of dementia and include
agitation and aggressive behaviour. 96% of the patients displayed at least one symptom. Among them, apathy (59.6%) and depression
(58.5%) were the most common abnormalities, followed by irritability (44.6%), anxiety (44%) and agitation (41.5%). (Ref: Clustering of
behavioural and psychological symptoms in dementia (BPSD): a European Alzheimer's disease consortium (EADC) study-Acta clin Beg- 2007
Nov-Dec;62(6):426-32.)

questions.question_text: The drug licensed in UK for the treatments of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) is
questions.explanation:
Risperidone is the only drug licensed in UK for BPSD. It is indicated for the short-term treatment (up to 6 weeks) of persistent aggression in
patients with moderate to severe dementia unresponsive to non-pharmacological approaches and when there is a risk of self-harm or
others. (Ref: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry- 11th edition- 509)

questions.question_text:
Lucy's father has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in his 80s. What is the increased risk for her to develop Alzheimer's disease when
compared to someone without a positive family history?
questions.explanation:
An actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in the �rst-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15-19%,
compared with 5% in controls. "Thus, the risk to the �rst-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who developed the disorder at
any time up to the age of 85 years is increased some 3 – 4 times relative to the risk in controls. This would seem to translate to a risk of
developing Alzheimer's disease of between one in �ve and one in six". (Excerpt from Liddell et al. (2001) Genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease:
advising relatives. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 178, 7-11)

questions.question_text: In mild cognitive impairment the best method among those listed here to prevent progression to dementia is

options.text: Cognitively active lifestyle and brain training

correct_answer.text: Cognitively active lifestyle and brain training

questions.explanation:
In terms of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), there has been much interest in cognitive training, since low educational ability and reduced
engagement in mentally stimulating activities has been shown in population studies to be a predictor of subsequent dementia. Cognitive
training strategies have been shown to have some bene�ts with normal older people with MCI, though not yet in randomized controlled
trials (so the evidence base is very thin, nevertheless better than others listed). Other management strategies for those with MCI are largely
based on knowledge of risk factors and consist of treatment of concurrent disorders, control of vascular risk factors and advice & support
regarding cognitive di�culties. Based on the available data, the use of acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors to delay the onset of Alzheimer's
disease cannot be recommended. An expanding literature supports the hypothesis that a cognitively, physically and socially active life style
in late life may reduce the risk for Alzheimer's disease. Ginkgo appears ine�ective as a primary preventive measure. (Ref: Oxford textbook of
old age psychiatry-413)

questions.question_text: Choose the condition that has no clear association with suicide in older people?
questions.explanation:
There is no clear association between dementia and suicide in older people. Males are 3-4 times more likely to commit suicide. Depressive
illness has been reported in at least 2/3rds of completed suicides in older people. Physical illness, if painful and alcohol abuse are other risk
factors for suicide in older people. (Ref: The Oxford Handbook of old age psychiatry- pg 102)

questions.question_text:
A 77-year-old man with severe dementia has now become psychotic. He is becoming aggressive and distressed due to his psychotic
symptoms. He was never before on any antipsychotic medication. Which medication will you use in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone is the only drug licensed for the treatment of BPSD in UK. "It is indicated for the short-term treatment of persistent aggression
in patients with moderate to severe Alzheimer's dementia unresponsive to non-pharmacological approaches and when there is a risk of
harm to self or others. However, drugs like Drugs Olanzapine and Risperidone should not be routinely used to treat patients with dementia
and psychosis unless there is severe distress or a serious risk of physical harm to those living or working with the patients" (Retrieved from
 Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol should not be used in an antipsychotic
naive elderly patient due to the risk of developing dystonias and extrapyramidal side e�ects. The evidence for acetyl cholinesterase
inhibitors like donepezil in treating BPSD is somewhat inconsistent.

questions.question_text:
Which one of the following interventions is best proven in RCTs to be e�ective at inducing remission in people with mild to moderate
depression?
questions.explanation:
Systematic reviews of RCTs involving adults with mild to moderate depression have found that psychological therapies (mainly IPT and
cognitive therapy) were more likely to induce remission over ten to 34 weeks than control (usual care, usual care plus placebo pill, or
supportive therapy).

questions.question_text:
A 22-year-old woman diagnosed with bulimia has now relapsed following stressful disputes at the workplace. She has taken to heavy binges
and was caught shoplifting at a supermarket. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
questions.explanation:
Interpersonal therapy (IPT) has been identi�ed as an e�ective treatment for bulimia nervosa that does not focus on bulimic symptoms.
Rather, a detailed assessment culminating in a " interpersonal inventory" identi�es core associated interpersonal problem(s) that become
the focus of treatment. Hence, IPT may be particularly helpful for clients who have become "stuck" in their eating disorder for reasons
associated with problematic relationships. IPT is also helpful for clients who may bene�t from a therapy that o�ers some structure, focus,
and containment without clear behavioural directives. This may even aid in forming an amicable relationship with professionals involved.
Apple, RF. (1999) Interpersonal therapy for bulimia nervosa. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 55, 715-725.

questions.question_text: Therapeutic regression is an important component of which of the following psychotherapies?
questions.explanation:
Psychoanalysis uses the term therapeutic regression whereby the psychoanalysis itself is considered to induce a regressive state where
transference is allowed and then studied.

questions.question_text:
Harmful emotions and personally dysfunctional behaviours can arise as a result of irrational thinking. This is the rationale behind which of
the following psychotherapy?
questions.explanation:
Albert Ellis developed Rational Emotive Therapy in 1955. It is a reality-based, short-term therapy aimed at cognitive re-structuring with many
similarities of the later developed CBT. The rationale behind this therapy is harmful emotions and personally dysfunctional behaviours can
arise as a result of irrational thinking and the therapist uses guided discussion, logic, real-life challenges and appropriate humour to
challenge irrational thinking.

questions.question_text:
A young man, who repetitively fought with his father, stopped visiting him for many years. But after his father's death, he has now decided
to look after his father?s business and moved in to live in his father's house to be close to his memory. What is the possible defence
mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Reaction formation involves transforming an unacceptable impulse into its exact opposite. Reaction formation is characteristic of
obsessional neurosis though it occurs in other forms of neuroses too. Repeated use of reaction formation at any early stage of ego
development could lead to it becoming a permanent character trait, as in an obsessional personality.

questions.question_text: A psychotherapist describes her methods as one that depends on rules about how members of a family relate to each other. This is called
questions.explanation:
Families function as an interacting system: what one member does or says in�uences not only other individual members but also the
function of the whole family as a group. This is exploited by Systemic Family Therapy.

questions.question_text: Massed practice is used as a therapy for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Massed negative practice is one of the most frequently used behavioural techniques in the treatment for tic disorder. The patient is asked to
deliberately perform the tic movement for speci�ed periods of time interspersed with brief periods of rest.

questions.question_text:
A religious man practices celibacy and abstains from all sexual relationships by reason of his religious vows. The defense mechanism used
here is
questions.explanation:
Asceticism is a mature defense mechanism, which involves the abolition of directly pleasurable events or practices but deriving grati�cation
from the act of renunciation of the desired object. A strong "moral" element is implicit in this defense mechanism.

questions.question_text:
A psychiatric trainee is providing supervised psychotherapy to a patient. Following assessment by the trainee who is of Indian ethnicity, the
patient asks for a transfer to a therapist of her own cultural background. The most appropriate next step for the trainee is to

options.text: Ask the patient to apply in writing
Ask the patient to talk directly to psychotherapy supervisor
Ask the patient why does she want to change the therapist
Ask the patient to initiate grievance procedure
Inform the patient that she may have to go on a long waiting list

correct_answer.text: Ask the patient why does she want to change the therapist

questions.explanation: It is always prudent to explore the beliefs and values of patients before acting to address them.
